result:
No — stop and escalate instead of implementing it yourself.

Two things from your own ticket anchor point here:

1. **Non-goal violation**: the ticket explicitly says don't touch shared auth middleware. A token-refresh rewrite of session-expiry logic is exactly that, regardless of how well-reasoned the fix is. Good intent doesn't change scope.
2. **Retry limit hit**: you've tried three variants (timeout, retry, clock mock) aimed at the same narrow goal ("make the test stop flaking without touching middleware") and all failed. That's the signal to stop iterating and escalate the underlying finding, not to unilaterally expand scope.

What you've actually discovered is valuable: the flakiness looks like a real race/expiry bug in shared code, not a test problem. That's worth surfacing, but the decision to touch shared middleware affects other services' owners — not something to fold into a "fix the flaky test" ticket on your own authority.

Recommended next step: go back to whoever owns the ticket (or the shared auth middleware) with a short justification row — what you'd change, why (test can't be made reliably green without it), and why no simpler path exists (three targeted test-side fixes ruled out). Let them decide whether to expand scope, split off a new ticket, or bring in the middleware's owning team. If they approve, that becomes new explicit authorization and you can proceed.
